Honolulu
December 1, 1952
Dear FamiLy,
We really feel now that we're home, even though we're
still 5,000 miles from New York.
No more Customs formalities; no
more forms to fill out; no more currencies to convert to dollars
or vice versa (with a liberal cut for the bankers both ways!)
If we should have to sum up our impressions of a round
the world trip in one word it would be "chenge".
Nothing is the
same.
Everything is different.
Old timers who
cannot adjust their
lives to the changes which heve taken place can be best classified
by that British slang expression,
"They've had it".
In Manila one
such ectually said to me, "These Filipinos have become absolutely
impossible - the way they act you'd think they owned the place!"
However, the policy or lack of policy, of the Trumen
administration has kept pace with all the changes. It has swept
like a weather-vane,
responsive to every wind that blows and much
of the wind has been from politicians.
Seemingly the only consistent
policy has been bused on the idea that if we give away enough
dollars welll make friends and influence people. Harry has sent his
emissaries - usually lame duck politicos or unsuccessful haberdashers -
to every corner of the world. Most of them carry satchels full of
checks signed by Harry or one of his agencies.
They set up elaborate
offices staffed with ne'er-do-well theorists and professional do-
gooders.
They rent the best houses and offices at prices well
above the going rates,
to the consternation of local businessmen.
They hire the best trained servants also at wages well above average
to the greater consternation of the local businessman's wife.
They
rate U.S. Conmissary privileges which means that they and their
families buy provisions for half the price paid by those poor tax-
payers who are trying to make a living in that community.
They en-
tertain with whiskey at two dollars a bottle and American cigarettes
. 60¢ per carton, while the local housewife pays five times that
They set up such an elaborate orgenization that most of
the funds go to support staft, and the latter never having "had it
so good" and not knowing how long it will last are more intent on
conserving the dollars then putting them out.
That is all to the
good under the cockeyed circumstances because it is certainly true
that we lose respect in oriental countries by giving money away.
If we loan it, as in the Philippines, the Filipinos resent the fact
that they must depend on American doles and at the same time despise
us for being so niggardly. It's the old story if you lend money
to a friend you lose your money and your friend.

He replied,
thanking me for the idea which he had passed along to the cartoonists
and then added a postscript, "That have you got agsinst baboons?"
on the last leg of
our trip around the world it is
with a profound sigh of relief and a heartfelt "Thank God" that we
return to a United States with IKE at the controls of the Ship of
State instead of that untrained Missouri chimpanzee.
Honolulu is wonderful. A few of you in the know will
admit that
the Royal Hawaiian is
somewhat better then the Trocadero
at Bangkok! Te had s fine trip from Manila with two Thanksgiving
Deys as the doy we gained crossing the date line was Thursday.
Approaching voke the pilot let me sit in the "jump seat" right
beside him and made a swing around the island so that 1 could see
the extent of damage done by the recent typhoon. It was extensive.
Most of the old quonset huts had been blown away and parts were
strewn all over the island. Our own facilities with the aid of a
little "moonlight requisition" had been jully restored but most of
the other personnel, largely C.A.A. employees, were still in tents.
We leave here Thursday December 4th for San Francisco
and hope to see most of you soon after this letter arrives.
All the best to all of you.
H. N. B.
